editorNote: Network addresses, home cockpits and a word processor worth typing.
morningLine: A new commercial network address enters the register; Connecticut gets a packet-switched dial-up route.

lead.headline: Symbolics registers the first .com address
body: Massachusetts workstation maker Symbolics registered symbolics.com on March 15, establishing the first registration under the .com domain. It is a small administrative entry in computer networking, rather than the opening of a new public information service.

The company comes out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology artificial-intelligence community and builds Lisp workstations for software development. Its 3600-series machines serve a specialized market, far from the home-computer cartridge counter.

The precise distinction is first .com registration, not first domain name of any kind. The new entry gives this commercial computer maker an address in the domain-name system; it should not be confused with a dial-up service such as CompuServe.

For readers watching the connections between computers, the register supplies this week’s noteworthy date. At the other end of the telephone line, Connecticut’s new ConnNet service offers a more immediate route to established information providers.
lead.dek: The Lisp-workstation maker enters the domain register on March 15.

stories.headline: Solo Flight makes the home computer a mail pilot’s cockpit
body: Solo Flight turns the joystick into a control column and the home screen into a cockpit. Arthur Leyenberger’s March COMPUTE! review examines Sid Meier’s MicroProse simulation for Commodore 64 and Atari computers with at least 48K, a disk drive and a joystick; the listed price is $34.95.

The flying includes takeoffs, landings, navigation and instrument work, with both a three-dimensional view and an instrument panel. Kansas is the gentlest territory, while Colorado’s mountains make a more demanding course; Washington is another available region.

Mail Pilot adds a working assignment: deliver five bags of mail while balancing fuel and payload. Its 21 airports and scoring for navigation, elapsed time, landings and delivered mail make the trip more than sightseeing. Worsening weather and, at higher difficulty, equipment failures keep the pilot occupied.

stories.headline: ConnNet opens Connecticut dial-up route to information services
body: Southern New England Telephone opened ConnNet on March 11, offering Connecticut customers a local public packet-switched route to established information services. CompuServe, NewsNet, Dow Jones News Retrieval and the National Library of Medicine are among the destinations.

Dial-up service runs at 300 to 1,200 bits per second. Dedicated business connections offer 4,800 to 56,000 bits per second, and employers can connect mainframes for remote employee access. ConnNet uses X.25 packet switching; it is not a new home-computer software package, and verified local access prices are not available here.

stories.headline: SpeedScript 3.0 puts a substantial word processor in a magazine
body: Charles Brannon’s SpeedScript 3.0 gives the Commodore 64 a machine-language word processor in the March issue of COMPUTE!. About 6K of program leaves more than 43K for text, described as roughly 20 to 40 printed pages.

Word wrap, search and replace, copying and moving text, adjustable margins, headers and footers bring substantial editing tools to the keyboard. Files can go to disk or tape. The revision incorporates a year of enhancements and debugging since the original GAZETTE version.

Readers can enter the complete listing with MLX or order the C64 disk for $12.95 plus $2 domestic shipping and handling. An earlier version cannot simply be patched into 3.0. VIC-20, Atari and Apple II editions are promised for later issues, not supplied by this listing.

stories.headline: Color printing moves below $300
body: Okidata’s March product notices put two printer prices below $300: the $268 Okimate 20 and the $299 Microline 182. These are published product prices, with interface-kit costs not established.

The Okimate 20 uses thermal transfer for color screen dumps on IBM PCs and compatibles, with Learn to Print and Color Screen Print included. The notice rates it at 80 characters per second in draft and 40 in its letter-quality mode. The Microline 182 dot-matrix model is described for IBM and Apple machines, at 120 cps utility and 60 enhanced.

market.headline: Faster modems face a supply squeeze
market.summary: March COMPUTE! reports $800–$900 prices for 2400-bps modems and a QAM-chip bottleneck. Its expectation of limited supply until fall is a contemporary forecast, not a confirmed outcome.

worldAnchor.headline: Gorbachev chosen to lead Soviet Communist Party
worldAnchor.summary: Mikhail Gorbachev was chosen to lead the Soviet Communist Party on March 11, succeeding Konstantin Chernenko. The Politburo minutes record Andrei Gromyko proposing him without dissenting voices.

bbsNote.headline: 2400-bps ambitions meet chip shortages and electronic junk mail
bbsNote.summary: March 1985 COMPUTE! column by Arlan R. Levitan, The Race To Talk Fast: 2400-bps modems, growing commercial online communities, and complaints about paying connect time to retrieve unwanted advertisements. All posts below are editorial paraphrases of published reporting, not recovered BBS messages.

posts.text: Hayes, Novation, U.S. Robotics, Racal-Vadic, Multitech, CTS Datacomm, Anderson Jacobson, Cermetek and Telenetics announced 2400-bps units at the previous November COMDEX. The column reports $800–$900 prices and a QAM-chip bottleneck; March/April online-service rollouts are forecasts.
Bob Walter is identified as sysop of the new Health Forum, moderating fitness discussions.
Billiam Coronel’s Comedy By Wire offers computer humor, with back issues available.

Levitan reports complaints about People/Link promotion. People/Link interpreted a removal statement as deletion of email; CompuServe denied deleting email and said it enforced its policy against commercial SIG messages. The distinction and dispute must be preserved.
Levitan objects that automatically retrieved unsolicited email consumes paid connection time. This is a dated complaint, not a claim to have identified the first spam message.

curiosity.headline: An $89.95 Apple board remembers ten seconds of your voice
curiosity.summary: Covox’s Voice Master brings small-scale recorded speech to the Apple IIe.
curiosity.detail: March COMPUTE! says the board can digitally record up to ten seconds and recall up to 64 numbered words, phrases or other sounds with BASIC commands. Vocabularies can be stored on disk or tape; microphone and software are included. It is recorded natural speech, not evidence of unlimited text-to-speech.
